grh_95842bedcde42bf5f00f.title: Suddenly Its Spring
paragraphs: Husband-and-wife lawyers Peter and Mary Morley return from wartime service after years apart only to discover that distance, pride and unspoken hurt have left their marriage close to divorce. Mary wants Peter to sign a divorce consent, while Peter realizes that he still loves her and tries a series of increasingly foolish schemes to make himself repulsive enough that she will decide against leaving him for another man. Their games produce jealousy, public embarrassment and competing romantic plans, but eventually Peter signs the papers because he believes Mary truly wants her freedom. As they divide the possessions in their apartment, each old object brings back a memory and exposes the misunderstandings they never discussed, including their grief over not having a child and the possibility that they could have adopted. A broken music box begins playing after being shaken, giving them an obvious metaphor for their own marriage. Mary finally dismisses the other man, and she and Peter abandon the divorce and reconcile.

This [[show|screen-directors-playhouse|Screen Directors Playhouse]] broadcast aired on March 27, 1949. It is listed as episode 12 in the archive. [[org|org.f2f0561f0ce2ddc5|NBC Radio Network]] carried the broadcast. The cast includes Fred MacMurray, [[person|virginia-gregg|Virginia Gregg]], Mitchell Leisen, [[person|frank-lovejoy|Frank Lovejoy]], and Hal Girard. Other credited names include Milton Geiger as radio adaptor and Frank Barton as announcer.
The surviving recording runs about 30 minutes.
This version presents a radio version of [[work|work.sdp.film.9f9dd66705d9fad5|Suddenly Its Spring]]. Milton Geiger adapted it for radio.

grh_958286a742bb71a01a4c.title: Only Yesterday
paragraphs: In World War I, young Mary Lane secretly marries soldier Jim Emerson just before his regiment is sent overseas. Mary soon learns she is pregnant and moves to New York, where she gives birth to their son while waiting for Jim to come home. But a wartime concussion leaves Jim with shell shock and large gaps in his memory, including his marriage to Mary, and she raises their son without him while sending unsigned New Year greetings year after year. On the eve of the 1929 crash they meet again as strangers and are instinctively drawn to each other, though Jim still cannot place her. Years later, as Mary is dying, a final letter reaches Jim and restores the missing truth. He comes to her bedside, recognizes the love he lost, and meets their son at last, beginning the father-son relationship Mary had waited years to make possible.

Other credited names include Bill Cairn as director, Nat Wolff as radio adaptor, and Jimmy Wallington as announcer.

grh_95866331a747e212819f.title: It Happens Every Spring
paragraphs: College chemistry professor Vernon Simpson accidentally creates a substance that makes baseballs behave impossibly around wooden bats. Keeping his discovery secret, he joins a major-league club under an assumed identity and becomes a sensational pitcher whose baffling delivery carries the team toward the pennant while his university colleagues and sweetheart wonder where he disappeared. When the chemical supply runs out, Vernon believes his career is finished, only to discover in the final game that he can still pitch well without it. He returns to the university with baseball earnings, his scientific future restored, and his romance intact.

grh_95b0e11bda427bcecac3.title: The Tell Tale Pigeon Feathers
paragraphs: Pigeon feathers in a boarding-house room lead Holmes to a carrier-pigeon espionage ring sending military information abroad. After decoding a report on troops at Aldershot, Holmes sends a false message to draw one agent to a music hall, but another member of the ring shoots the man and Watson is arrested while holding his revolver. Police surgeon Dr. Hendricks then fabricates powder burns to strengthen the case against Watson. Holmes shows that only the surgeon could have fired a blank into the corpse and removed the telltale wadding during the autopsy, then bluffs Hendricks into betraying himself with a reference to pigeon feathers.

grh_95f6476927a31d0aec52.title: Words at War 43-12-14 (27) Mother America
paragraphs: A dramatization of Carlos P. Romulo's Mother America frames the fall of Bataan and Corregidor within a broader account of the American relationship with the Philippines. Romulo traces the islands from colonial rule through expanded schools, health programs, infrastructure, political participation and the Filipino demand for eventual independence, arguing that democratic guidance should lead toward self-government rather than permanent domination. He closes by presenting Philippine independence as a model for a postwar world in which freedom, education and fair treatment replace imperial rule.
